classification.difficultyReason: Find the original intercepts and vertex, substitute −x with the correct square, and transfer the features to the opposite side of the y-axis on the same axes.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$, labelling the vertex and $x$-intercepts.

answer.short: Downward-opening parabola with vertex $(2,4)$ and $x$-intercepts $(0,0)$ and $(4,0)$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y&=4x-x^2\\y&=x(4-x)\end{align*}$$
At $y=0$, the roots are $x=0$ and $x=4$. The axis of symmetry is halfway between them at $x=2$.
$$\begin{align*}f(2)&=4(2)-2^2\\f(2)&=4\end{align*}$$
Sketch the downward-opening parabola through $(0,0)$ and $(4,0)$ with vertex $(2,4)$. Use these axes again in part (b).

spec.sourceRegion: Answer book, printed page 368, Exercise 9A Q3(a)
spec.description: Downward-opening parabola with dashed guides to its vertex.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Simplify the equation $y=f(-x)$ and sketch the graph on the same set of axes using a different coloured pen, labelling the new vertex and $x$-intercepts.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}y&=f(-x)\\y&=4(-x)-(-x)^2\\y&=-4x-x^2\end{align*}$$
On the axes from part (a), reflect the vertex $(2,4)$ to $(-2,4)$ and the intercept $(4,0)$ to $(-4,0)$. The origin stays fixed. Sketch the reflected downward-opening parabola in a different colour.

spec.sourceRegion: Answer book, printed page 368, Exercise 9A Q3(b)
spec.description: Common axes with the original curve blue dashed on the right and the reflected curve red solid on the left. The reflected vertex guide meets the x-axis at the corrected label −2.
spec.mathematics: y=4x−x² and y=−4x−x² share (0,0). The reflection sends (2,4) to (−2,4) and (4,0) to (−4,0).

children.label: c
children.prompt: What is the relationship between the graph of $y=f(x)$ and $y=f(-x)$?

answer.short: They are reflections of each other across the $y$-axis.
answer.worked: A point $(x,f(x))$ on the original graph corresponds to $(-x,f(x))$ on the new graph, since $f(-(-x))=f(x)$. Only the sign of the $x$-coordinate changes, so the reflection is across the $y$-axis.
